hazards.messy-bunk-hazard: That rest bunk still has the last crew member's bedding on it. A rest facility that isn't actually reset between users is a rest facility the next tired crew member cannot trust is even clean, let alone quiet enough to actually rest in.
hazards.noise-source-hazard: That equipment is running loudly right next to the rest area. A rest period spent next to a noise nobody addressed is not actually rest, whatever the schedule says this crew member was given the time for.
hazards.pressure-not-to-report-decoy: That note says the flight needs covering, so don't call in fatigued. A no-fault fatigue report exists specifically so a genuinely tired crew member can say so without a schedule pressure like this one weighing against it — the pressure is the thing that gets ignored here, not the honest report.
hazards.untested-alarm-decoy: That wake alarm has never actually been tested. A rest period that ends on an alarm nobody confirmed works is a rest period that might not end when this crew member actually needs it to.

interrupts.alert: Crew scheduling calls mid-rest asking this crew member to extend today's duty to cover a gap.
interrupts.cue: That gets deferred to the fatigue policy, not agreed to on the spot.
interrupts.kind: Scheduling calls asking for a duty extension
interrupts.missNote: The extension got agreed to on the spot, mid-rest, with no reference to the fatigue policy at all. That's the exact pressure this policy was written to take out of one tired crew member's hands.
interrupts.why: Agreeing to an extension mid-rest, before the rest period is even finished, is exactly the kind of pressure the fatigue policy exists to answer instead of this crew member's own instinct to help out — the honest answer is checking the policy, not saying yes to make scheduling's problem go away.
interrupts.wrongNote: Defer to the fatigue policy — this isn't a decision to make on the phone mid-rest.

interrupts.alert: The primary wake alarm fails to sound as the rest period is ending.
interrupts.cue: That's exactly why a backup method exists — use it now.
interrupts.kind: The wake alarm fails during the actual rest period
interrupts.missNote: The failed alarm went unaddressed with no backup used. A single point of failure on something this important is exactly what a backup method exists to catch.
interrupts.why: A tested primary alarm that still fails is not a reason to skip waking up on time — it's exactly the situation the backup method exists for, and using it immediately is what keeps one equipment failure from turning into a missed sign-in.
interrupts.wrongNote: Use the backup wake method now — a failed primary alarm is exactly why it exists.

lateNotes.brief-relief-crew: Hold that. The self-check has to actually be complete before there's anything honest to hand off to relief crew.
lateNotes.fatigue-report-line: Not yet — the self-assessment comes first. Whether this call is even needed depends on being honest about that first.

name: Fatigue and Duty-Time Self-Check

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Open the airline's own fatigue policy before signing in for duty.
steps.prompt: Open the airline's own fatigue policy before signing in for duty.
steps.title: Pull the fatigue risk management policy
steps.why: This policy is what actually defines every threshold this station respects — reading it first is what keeps this self-check honest to the airline's own standard instead of this crew member's own guess at what's probably fine.

steps.cue: Answer the self-assessment honestly before signing in for duty.
steps.prompt: Answer the self-assessment honestly before signing in for duty.
steps.title: Complete the alertness self-assessment
steps.why: This self-assessment only protects anyone if it's answered honestly — a crew member who talks themselves into a better answer than the one that's actually true has removed the one check standing between fatigue and a flight this crew member should not have signed in for.

steps.cue: Review the sleep log and log today's commute time before relying on the self-assessment alone.
steps.prompt: Review the sleep log and log today's commute time before relying on the self-assessment alone.
steps.title: Review the factors behind the number
steps.why: The self-assessment score means more once it's read against what's actually behind it — the sleep log and the commute time are the two facts this crew member has that the score alone doesn't carry on its own.

steps.cue: Two things about this rest area aren't right. Find them before trusting it for real rest.

itemNames.messy-bunk: a rest bunk that wasn't reset for the next crew member
itemNames.noise-source: loud equipment running next to the rest area

itemNotes.messy-bunk: This gets reset now — a bunk left as the last user left it is not actually ready for whoever needs it next.
itemNotes.noise-source: This gets flagged and addressed — a rest area next to something this loud isn't actually a rest area, whatever it's labelled.

steps.prompt: Two things about this rest area aren't right. Find them before trusting it for real rest.
steps.title: Scan the rest area before using it
steps.why: A rest period only does what it's meant to if the facility it happens in actually supports rest — this scan is what catches the difference between a rest area on paper and one that actually works before this crew member is relying on it.

steps.cue: Confirm the bunk, the curtain and the temperature are all actually set for rest.
steps.prompt: Confirm the bunk, the curtain and the temperature are all actually set for rest.
steps.title: Confirm the rest facility is ready
steps.why: Confirming this now, before lying down, is what turns a facility that's merely available into one this crew member can actually count on for the rest period it's meant to provide.

steps.cue: Hold the test button and confirm the wake alarm actually sounds before relying on it.
steps.holdBreakNote: Let go before the alarm actually sounded. An untested alarm is exactly the kind of assumption this rest period cannot afford to rely on.
steps.prompt: Hold the test button and confirm the wake alarm actually sounds before relying on it.
steps.title: Test the wake alarm
steps.why: An alarm that looks set and an alarm that's actually confirmed to sound are two different facts, and the only way to know the second one is true is testing it now, not trusting it for the one moment it actually has to work.

steps.cue: Turn the dial to a comfortable setting for actual rest, per the facility's own controls.
steps.prompt: Turn the dial to a comfortable setting for actual rest, per the facility's own controls.
steps.title: Set the rest area temperature
steps.why: A rest period spent too hot or too cold to actually settle into sleep is a rest period that only counted on the schedule, not in practice — setting this now is a small step that makes the difference between the two.

steps.cue: Check the fatigue risk indicator and read it honestly against the self-assessment already given.

gauge.label: FATIGUE RISK
gauge.missNote: Signed in without reading this indicator honestly against the self-assessment. A risk indicator only helps if its reading is actually looked at before, not after, signing in.

steps.prompt: Check the fatigue risk indicator and read it honestly against the self-assessment already given.
steps.title: Read the fatigue risk indicator
steps.why: This indicator exists to be read honestly against the self-assessment this crew member already gave — it only protects anyone if the reading that comes back elevated is actually acted on, not glossed over on the way to signing in.

steps.cue: Keep the vigilance indicator steady in the target band for the whole check.
steps.holdBreakNote: Attention lapsed during the check. A vigilance check that drifts out of band is exactly the kind of early signal this self-check is designed to surface.
steps.prompt: Keep the vigilance indicator steady in the target band for the whole check.
steps.title: Complete the brief vigilance check
steps.why: A brief, steady vigilance check is a second honest data point alongside the self-assessment — attention that keeps lapsing here is worth noticing now, in a training exercise, rather than for the first time on an actual flight.

steps.cue: Call the no-fault fatigue reporting line the moment the self-check calls for it — no hesitation.
steps.prompt: Call the no-fault fatigue reporting line the moment the self-check calls for it — no hesitation.
steps.title: Call the no-fault fatigue line if needed
steps.why: This line exists specifically so a genuinely tired crew member can say so without it counting against them — using it the moment it's actually called for is the entire point of building a no-fault system in the first place.

steps.cue: Record the actual start and end times for this duty period in the logbook.
steps.prompt: Record the actual start and end times for this duty period in the logbook.
steps.title: Log the duty time
steps.why: An honest, actual-time log is what the airline's own fatigue policy is checked against later — a log that rounds favorably or gets filled in from memory afterward is a log that can no longer be trusted to catch a pattern building over several duty periods.

steps.cue: Brief the relief crew member on the handoff, then confirm — honestly — that they're actually alert enough to take over.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Brief first, then confirm alertness — asking about fitness before the handoff has even been explained skips the context that question needs.
steps.prompt: Brief the relief crew member on the handoff, then confirm — honestly — that they're actually alert enough to take over.
steps.title: Brief relief crew, then confirm they're alert
steps.why: A handoff briefing that skips the honest question about alertness hands off a risk along with the job — confirming it out loud, after the briefing, is what makes this crew member's own honesty about fitness for duty something the next person actually benefits from too.

steps.cue: Record that the self-check was completed, including anything flagged.
steps.prompt: Record that the self-check was completed, including anything flagged.
steps.title: Log the self-check
steps.why: This log is what lets the airline's own fatigue risk management program see patterns across many crew members over time — a self-check that was actually done but never logged is invisible to the one system built to catch problems this platform, or any one flight, cannot see on its own.

supportLine: your AFA-CWA or ALPA local's member assistance resources, or the airline's own employee assistance line — fatigue is a safety issue this crew's own unions built a no-fault reporting line to actually hear about
